newsitem.title: UK: FTSE may fall to 3,800 before stablising - chartists.
newsitem.headline: FTSE may fall to 3,800 before stablising - chartists.

text.p: The current correction in the London stock market is not yet over and prices may turn lower in the months ahead before levelling out, technical chart analysts said on Wednesday.
The market, as measured by the FTSE 100 index of blue chip shares, has lost around four percent in the past four weeks from its intra-day record of 4,466.
"It could now go down to 3,800," said Chris Chaitow, technical analyst at Robert Fleming Securities, adding that the market's fortunes were strictly limited by the actions on Wall Street.

"The FTSE is about 80 percent correlated to Wall Street," said Chaitow. The likelihood of higher interest rates in the United States painted a bearish medium-term picture for U.S. equities, which in turn would affect British stocks similarly.
From charts going back 30 years, Chaitow estimated that the British market followed a cycle taking 37 months to complete between each cyclical low point.
"The average fall (between high-to-low points) is 15 to 20 percent," said Chaitow. "And the last cycle low was in the summer of 1994 (when the index was around 2,930)."
A 15 percent correction for the FTSE from its March peak implies a move down to 3,800. "Our recommendation is to sell into strength up to July and then keep out (of the market)," said Chaitow.
Sectors such as banks, media and pharmaceuticals which have driven the market might be spurned as investors switched attention to more defensive groups, he said.

These defensive groups include shares in companies such as Guinness Plc, which is in the alcoholic beverage sector, Unilever Plc -- in food and household goods manufacturing -- and Reckitt & Colman Plc in household goods.
Another sector to avoid is engineering, said Chaitow.

Richard Marshall, a director at Investment Research of Cambridge Ltd, believes British equities will shadow Wall Street which in turn will shadow the bond market as they head lower. But he is less pessimistic than Chaitow.

The U.S. long bond hit chart support at 7.13 percent on Tuesday and if this level held, the Dow Jones industrial average should find support around 6,400-6,600 points, said Marshall. It closed at 6,611 on Tuesday.
"The Dow should then stabilise and might even edge higher," he added, implying a similar scenario for the FTSE.
U.S. interest rates might rise again but he did not believe this would happen as often as when rates last rose in 1994, which caused a severe setback for U.S and British equities.

"In 1994, U.S. interest rates rose seven times. It's not the same situation this time round. When Wall Street realises this, the markets will at least stabilise," he said. "It's only on falling interest rates that a bull market can continue."
The Dow could then range trade between 6,600-7,000 over the summer months before pushing higher.
The final leg of a bull market is usually one in which smaller capitalised stocks outperform the blue chips.

But Marshall said the bull leg in British equities from July 1996 showed no sign of smaller stocks doing better than blue chips. There should still be scope for a further slight gain in the FTSE later in the year.

He expected market volatility to increase around the British election on May 1. Investors might prefer high yielding shares in this environment, but the current market leaders -- the banks, pharmaceuticals and oil companies -- would not lose out too much.

Forthcoming flotations of mutually-owned building societies as banks this summer would increase the weighting of the bank sector in the FTSE to around 20 percent from 11 percent. Index-tracking funds would have to increase their exposure to this sector, said Marshall.
The election would affect market volatility but not necessarily its direction, said Edward Menashy, economist at stockbrokers Charles Stanley & Co.
"Politics will act as catalyst which will affect the speed of the market but not its direction," said Menashy, who believes the FTSE could go down to 4,050 before the current weakness abates.

"It could pick up on news of a budget if, as expected, Labour wins," he said. But he doubted that the 4,466 peak would be overcome, predicting that the market would produce a bearish double-top chart pattern in which prices fall away after making a second peak.
"This is a market to sell into strength, and the bold will sell into further strength," said Menashy, saying investor portfolios should begin to be overweight in cash.
The time to get back into equities was when bond markets staged a revival, he added.
